title: Using inhibition of the adipogenesis of adipose-derived stem cells in vitro for toxicity prediction
author: Abud, Paschoal, et al.

steps.title: Plate AD‑MSC cells
steps.instruction: Plate human adipose‑derived mesenchymal stromal cells (AD‑MSCs) in 96‑well plates under standard culture conditions (37 °C, 5 % CO₂) using the appropriate growth medium.

steps.title: Prepare adipogenic induction medium
steps.instruction: Prepare adipogenic differentiation medium containing dexamethasone, insulin, indomethacin and 3‑isobutyl‑1‑methylxanthine (IBMX) at the concentrations recommended for AD‑MSC adipogenesis.

steps.title: Add test substances and SDS controls
steps.instruction: Add the test compounds (prepared as serial dilutions minutes before use) to the wells; include a separate plate with a series of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) concentrations as the external positive control of adipogenesis inhibition.

steps.title: Incubate for adipogenic differentiation
steps.instruction: Incubate the cells for 14 days, refreshing the induction medium as described in the schematic (50 µl per well of 2× induction medium in columns 2–11 and 100 µl per well of maintenance medium in columns 1 and 12). Maintain plates at 37 °C, 5 % CO₂.

steps.title: Fix cells (if required)
steps.instruction: After 14 days, fix the cells according to the laboratory’s standard fixation protocol before staining.

steps.title: Wash plates with PBS
steps.instruction: Wash each well twice with 1× PBS pre‑warmed to 37 °C (200 µl per wash).

steps.title: Stain with Nile red
steps.instruction: Prepare Nile red working solution by diluting the stock dye (1 mg ml⁻¹) 1:1000 in 1× PBS. Add 50 µl per well, incubate 30 min protected from direct light.

steps.title: Wash after Nile red
steps.instruction: Wash each well twice with 1× PBS pre‑warmed to 37 °C ± 1 °C (200 µl per wash).

steps.title: Stain nuclei with DAPI
steps.instruction: Add 50 µl per well of DAPI solution, incubate at room temperature for 10 min protected from direct light.

steps.title: Final washes and storage
steps.instruction: Wash three times with 1× PBS, then store the plates with buffer at 2–8 °C until imaging. Plates may be stored up to 15 days before data acquisition.

steps.title: Acquire fluorescence images
steps.instruction: If a high‑content imaging (HCI) microscope is available, scan the plates; otherwise use a plate reader (e.g., BioTek®) to record Nile red fluorescence (excitation 450–500 nm, emission >528 nm) and DAPI signal.

steps.title: Set up image analysis workflow
steps.instruction: Configure the HCI software as follows:

substeps.instruction: Identify nuclei using DAPI channel (channel 1) and exclude objects touching plate borders.
Identify cytoplasm using Nile red channel (channel 2).
Calculate cytoplasmic intensity properties for channel 3 (green Nile red staining).
Define adipose‑positive (Adipo⁺) cells by setting intensity cut‑offs between negative and positive populations.
Select results: nuclei count, % Adipo⁺ cells, sum area of Adipo⁺ cells, sum intensity of Adipo⁺ cells.
Save the image acquisition and analysis setup.
Apply the saved setup to the entire plate.
Export the data to a spreadsheet‑compatible format (e.g., Excel).
Proceed to statistical analysis as described below.

steps.title: Transfer readouts to spreadsheet
steps.instruction: Import the exported image‑analysis data into Microsoft Excel (or equivalent).

steps.title: Assess assay quality
steps.instruction: For each readout (nuclei number, % Adipo⁺ cells, sum area, sum intensity) calculate:

substeps.instruction: If |SSMD_robust| ≥ 3, the assay passes quality criteria.
Exclude the minimum and maximum values from each of the eight test‑concentration columns and from each of the two positive‑control columns.
Calculate mean and standard deviation for each remaining group.
Convert each mean to a percentage of the mean of the adipogenesis‑positive control.
Using GraphPad Prism® (or similar), fit the percentage data to a four‑parameter logistic (Hill) curve with variable slope, constraining the bottom parameter to 0.
Obtain EC₅₀, top, Hill slope, and R² from the fit.
logIC₅₀(corrected) = logEC₅₀ – log[(top – bottom)·Y – bottom – 1] / HillCoefficient, where Y = 50 % and bottom = 0.

steps.title: Combine IC₅₀ values
steps.instruction: Compute the geometric mean of all corrected IC₅₀ values from replicate assays: geometric mean = (∏ IC₅₀ᵢ)^(1/n), where n is the number of assays.

steps.title: Prepare test‑item dilutions
steps.instruction: Prepare serial dilutions of each test compound (hydrosoluble or non‑hydrosoluble) minutes before adding to cells. Also prepare a serial dilution series of SDS as the external positive control and include it on each plate.

description: Currently, there are several different methodologies to assess the toxicological effects of test chemicals on human cells and animal tissues in vitro and ex vivo. Researchers use 2D cell culture in many assays that have already been validated; however, these methods are limited, as they use nonhuman lineage cells that may have chromosomal anomalies or primary cells that have limitations in the number of passages and the variability between batches [1]. In this context, human stem cells have been explored as a valuable in vitro system for toxicological studies [2] as an alternative to using animals or traditional in vitro methods. Due to their advantages of self-renewal capability and cell differentiation, stem cells can be very useful for the evaluation of toxicological mechanisms. These specific characteristics may provide additional strategies and applicable data for human toxicity predictions and to improve sensitivity [3,4]. In addition, it is possible to carry out tests on different biological samples to evaluate biological variability [4], [5], [6], [7]. Moreover, stem cells derived from tissue removed during surgery, specifically liposuction procedures [4,8], are of great interest because they represent disposable material, are easy to handle, and do not require a wide variety of supplements to culture [9]. Given the advantages of stem cells as alternatives to animal models and the need to reduce animal usage, we describe a system that can be used to quantify adipogenesis in vitro and apply an adipogenesis-inhibition protocol to estimate toxicity adequately; we also predict the best-fit starting dose for animal testing with the acute toxic class (ATC) method [10]. The protocol described here first involves the cultivation of human adipose tissue-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (AD-MSCs) [11].
